note: Intravitreal anti-VEGF-A antibodies and fragments for neovascular AMD: the cynomolgus laser-CNV model is the field's textbook translational success, while the same species has been wrong about immune-mediated ocular inflammation in both directions.
label: Wet AMD (anti-VEGF)

engagement.note: Radiolabelled anti-VEGF Fab crossed the neural retina to the RPE within an hour in rhesus eyes; full-length IgG stopped at the inner limiting membrane.
engagement.short: Fab reaches RPE, IgG stops at ILM
engagement.quote: In contrast, the Fab antibody fragment diffused through the neural retina to the retinal pigment epithelial layer at the 1-hr time point and persisted in this location for up to 7 days.
engagement.judgement: Abstract-level reading (Toxicol Pathol, paywalled). The Fab dosed was the parent rhuMAb VEGF Fab, not ranibizumab itself, hence product_in_model false.

engagement.note: Label: CNV leakage on fluorescein angiography fell by month 3 in treated patients, the read-out the monkey laser-CNV model had used for ranibizumab.
engagement.quote: In patients treated with LUCENTIS, the area of vascular leakage, on average, decreased by Month 3 as assessed by fluorescein angiography.
engagement.reason: Leakage fell in patients as in monkeys
engagement.judgement: Same read-out (angiographic leakage from CNV) in monkeys (Krzystolik 2002; EMA 2007 scientific discussion: 'It was also shown that ranibizumab (0.5 mg every 2nd week) inhibited vascular leakage from the CNV-lesions.') and in patients, but the label does not itself cite the monkey result, so comparison_stated is false. The 1999 model's second prediction, that a full-length IgG would not reach the target, is deliberately not scored: off-label bevacizumab's clinical equivalence (CATT 2011) argues against it, but no primary source frames that as a model-versus-patient comparison.

dose.note: Anti-VEGF Fab half-life in rhesus vitreous 3.2 days (IgG 5.6); cynomolgus ranibizumab later ~3 days, called favourable for monthly injection (Gaudreault 2005).
dose.quote: The half-life in vitreous was 5.6 days for the full-length antibody and 3.2 days for the Fab antibody.
dose.judgement: Opens the strip with the parent Fab in rhesus; the pivotal product PK is Gaudreault 2005 (cynomolgus, doi:10.1167/iovs.04-0601: 'terminal half-life of approximately 3 days', 'favorable for ... monthly ITV injection'), not added as a separate entry because the status does not change.

dose.note: Label: vitreous half-life ~3 days in animals versus ~9 days in patients; the monthly 0.3-0.5 mg regimen built on the monkey figure held in MARINA/ANCHOR.
dose.short: Human half-life 9 d vs 3 d monkey
dose.quote: Based on the disappearance of ranibizumab from serum, the estimated average vitreous elimination half-life was approximately 9 days.
dose.judgement: Judgement call. The operative prediction from the monkey PK (Gaudreault 2005: ~3-day half-life, 'favorable for ... monthly ITV injection') held: 0.3 and 0.5 mg monthly both worked and the dose-response was flat. The PK parameter itself missed by ~3x in the conservative direction; section 12.3 of the same label states both numbers ('In animal studies, following intravitreal injection, ranibizumab was cleared from the vitreous with a half-life of approximately 3 days.'). Direct aqueous sampling later gave 7.19 days (Krohne 2012, doi:10.1016/j.ajo.2012.03.047) and population PK 9 days (Xu 2013, doi:10.1167/iovs.12-10260). A re-scorer who counts a >2x PK miss as a contradiction should flip this cell to contra.

efficacy.note: Ranibizumab (rhuFab V2) prevented laser-induced CNV in cynomolgus monkeys and reduced leakage from established lesions; the authors called it the nonclinical proof of principle.
efficacy.quote: Intravitreal rhuFab VEGF injections prevented formation of clinically significant CNV in cynomolgus monkeys and decreased leakage of already formed CNV with no significant toxic effects.
efficacy.judgement: Abstract-level reading (Arch Ophthalmol, paywalled). Laser CNV itself dates from Ryan 1979; 2002 is the first use with this drug class. The EMA scientific discussion (2007) names it as the submitted disease model, hence model_filed true.

efficacy.note: MARINA: 95% of ranibizumab patients lost <15 letters versus 62% on sham, mean gain ~7 letters; ANCHOR matched; the monkey model's prediction held.
efficacy.quote: At 12 months, 94.5% of the group given 0.3 mg of ranibizumab and 94.6% of those given 0.5 mg lost fewer than 15 letters, as compared with 62.2% of patients receiving sham injections (P<0.001 for both comparisons).
efficacy.reason: Monkey laser-CNV prediction held in MARINA/ANCHOR
efficacy.judgement: The trial paper does not itself cite the monkey model as far as I could verify (NEJM full text returned 403), so comparison_stated is false. The stated side-by-side accounts are the developers' own (Ferrara 2006, Retina, doi:10.1097/01.iae.0000242842.14624.e7, typed Review in PubMed) and the EMA scientific discussion (2007): 'The in vivo disease model used was the well established model of laser-induced CNV, in this case, in monkeys.' ANCHOR (Brown 2006, doi:10.1056/NEJMoa062655) gave the same answer against verteporfin. Endpoints are not commensurable (CNV incidence/leakage in monkeys vs letters in patients), hence direction_only. No failed anti-VEGF-A antibody was flagged by the model, so not neg; brolucizumab (HAWK/HARRIER, Dugel 2020, doi:10.1016/j.ophtha.2019.04.017) later kept matching on efficacy. Not scored: the monkey laser-CNV model also predicted an Ang-2 add-on benefit for faricimab that the non-inferiority phase 3 trials did not test; no primary source frames that as a miss.

safety.note: Every monkey eye developed transient anterior-chamber inflammation within 24 h of the first injection, milder on re-injection; no haemorrhage or other toxicity.
safety.short: Transient anterior-chamber inflammation in all monkeys
safety.quote: All eyes treated with rhuFab VEGF developed acute anterior chamber inflammation within 24 hours of the first injection that resolved within 1 week, and this inflammation was less severe with subsequent injections.

safety.note: EMA: monkeys showed dose-related, ADA-linked intraocular inflammation with perivascular sheathing; patients showed manageable inflammation (18% vs 11% control, serious uveitis 1.3%), no vasculitis.
safety.short: Inflammation matched; monkey vasculitis did not
safety.quote: However, the ocular inflammation was not alarming and easy to follow in the clinic, and reassurance has been given with the 2-year clinical data.
safety.judgement: Judgement call: same rather than contra. The monkey prediction the regulator acted on (injection- and ADA-related intraocular inflammation) appeared in patients: Lucentis 2006 label Table 1 intraocular inflammation 18%-5% vs 11%-3% control, and 'some patients with the highest levels of immunoreactivity were noted to have iritis or vitritis'; MARINA (doi:10.1056/NEJMoa054481): 'presumed endophthalmitis was identified in five patients (1.0%) and serious uveitis in six patients (1.3%)'. But the monkeys over-predicted severity and a vasculitis: 'Most monkeys with perivascular sheathing were positive for antibodies towards ranibizumab, indicating an immune-related effect which has not been observed clinically.' and 'the perivascular sheathing does not appear to be a useful marker for prediction of severe cases of inflammation in patients.' The applicant attributed the monkey picture to giving a humanised protein to animals; EMA: 'non-clinical data can give no assurance to the long-term clinical use.' A re-scorer who counts that false-positive vasculitis as a wrong prediction should flip this to contra. Source is an EMA (not FDA) review because the FDA review index for BLA 125156 returned 404; if EMA documents are disallowed, substitute Rosenfeld 2006 (comparison_stated false, year 2006) with the uveitis sentence above.

safety.note: Brolucizumab caused retinal vasculitis/occlusion in patients (HAWK/HARRIER post hoc: IOI 4.6%, vasculitis 3.3%, occlusion 2.1%); monkey toxicology, ADA-positive animals included, showed none.
safety.quote: This finding was inconsistent with preclinical studies in cynomolgus monkeys that demonstrated no drug-related intraocular inflammation, or RV/RO, despite the presence of preexisting and treatment-emergent antidrug antibodies (ADAs) in some animals.
safety.judgement: Comparison stated by the sponsor's own scientists; quote is in the abstract (full text paywalled). Patient-side numbers from the independent Safety Review Committee post hoc of HAWK/HARRIER (Mones 2021, doi:10.1016/j.ophtha.2020.11.011): definite/probable IOI 4.6%, IOI+vasculitis 3.3%, IOI+vasculitis+occlusion 2.1%, vs IOI 1.1% on aflibercept; first case series Baumal 2020 (doi:10.1016/j.ophtha.2020.04.017); Beovu 2019 label: IOI 4% vs 1%, retinal artery occlusion 1% vs <1%, ADA pre-treatment in 36%-52%, 'Intraocular inflammation was observed in 6% of patients with anti-brolucizumab antibodies'. Year is 2023 because that is when the model-versus-patient statement was published; events were reported in 2020. Karle also showed monkeys reproduce RV/RO only after adjuvant pre-immunisation to high ADA titres, i.e. the model could be made to show it after the fact. Contrast with 2007: for ranibizumab the same species over-predicted an ADA-driven vasculitis that patients never showed. The Beovu US label has no animal toxicology section (13.1 only), so model_filed is null; the EMA Beovu EPAR was not checked within budget. registry_date is the HAWK/HARRIER results-first-posted date (both 2019-10-31).
